subtopic: DEMOLITION OF HOUSES, DORCHESTER PENITENTIARY
DEMOLITION OF HOUSES, DORCHESTER PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
1.	Is the demolition of houses at Dorchester penitentiary, New Brunswick, undertaken with the approval of the government of Canada?
2.	Have the houses been condemned as being unsuitable for human habitation?
3.	If so, what is the name of the official who made such report?
4.	Has any attempt been made to sell the houses to tenants presently occupying same?
5.	Has any attempt been made to secure bids by public tender?
6.	What is the present appraised value of the houses to be destroyed?
7.	Will employees of the Department of Justice occupying these houses at present be obliged to secure housing accommodation elsewhere and, if so, will allowance for travelling be on a mileage basis?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: DEMOLITION OF HOUSES, DORCHESTER PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Parts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The demolition of houses at Dorchester was undertaken pursuant to a penitentiary service policy to phase out of government housing except in isolated localities. In October, 1963 two frame units were declared surplus to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation (CADC). As no offers to purchase these units were received CADC authorized the penitentiary service to dispose of these units, and in view of this experience CADC subsequently authorized the penitentiary service to proceed with the disposal of other frame units.
The units disposed of while not officially condemned were approximately eighty (80) years old, and the cost of maintenance of some of these units amounted to over $1,200 in a two year period. This cost of maintenance did not include any charge for labour, which was provided by the medium and minimum security inmates. However, this labour service will not be available in the future with the transfer of the minimum security inmates to the existing Springhill minimum security institution, and the transfer of medium security inmates to the new young offenders (medium
Questions
security) institution which will be opened at Springhill late in 1966.
In the opinion of experienced personnel within the penitentiary service, bearing in mind the age of the frame units, the state of disrepair, the monthly rentals, and the fact that they were situated on crown lands and would have to be removed in the event of sale, and the policy of the penitentiary service to phase out of housing, the cost of continued maintenance would not be justified.
Fixtures and other material salvaged in the disposal of these frame units is at present in storage and will be utilized by the penitentiary service as the occasion arises. In the circumstances no appraisals were obtained.
7. The employees of the department who occupied the demolished houses have secured housing accommodation elsewhere and, where otherwise qualified are entitled to an allowance for travelling under Treasury Board minute 608561, dated June 28, 1963.

speakeroldname: Miss Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of Slate):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ALTERATION IN TIMETABLE FOR COLOUR TRANSMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house may recall that last September the government announced its decision to implement the introduction of colour television in Canada by a three-stage process.
By this decision, stations prepared to undertake colour casting were permitted to commence test transmissions during the night-time period starting July I; to begin regular colour transmissions on a shakedown basis on October 1; and to have all colour transmissions up to full technical requirements by next January 1.

July 13. 1966
Television
This timetable was worked out in consultation with all interested parties and was accepted by them at that time. The primary consideration in setting the various dates was the need to allow sufficient time for the necessary technical installations and staff training.
In recent months, however, it has become apparent that technical preparations for colour casting are advancing within the industry on a much quicker basis than had been anticipated. In view of these developments, representations have been made to the government, particularly by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, to amend the colour timetable accordingly and especially to move up the October 1 date for full colour transmissions to coincide better with the start of fall program schedules.
The government has given consideration to these representations and, in view of the declared readiness of the various elements of the broadcasting industry to meet an earlier date, we are now prepared to authorize full colour transmissions as of September 1. The remaining four months of this year will continue to be treated as a shakedown period during which minor equipment and operating adjustments can be made in order that all technical requirements may be met as of January 1.
The decision to permit full colour transmissions is open to both the public and private sectors of the broadcasting industry. In the case of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, however there is a caveat. Any alteration in its plans will have to be carried out within the limits of operating and capital funds already approved for the current fiscal year. This is in keeping with the government's view on this subject as outlined in the white paper on broadcasting.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the advance of one month in the introductory date for full colour transmissions will be of value both to the broadcasters and to the viewing public in permitting both to enjoy the benefits of colour from the outset of the fall program season.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ALTERATION IN TIMETABLE FOR COLOUR TRANSMISSION
speechtext:
Members of this party heartily welcome the announcement which the hon. lady has just made with respect to colour telecasting in this country. We are delighted that technical developments as outlined by the minister have been proceeding faster than anticipated, and that the colour schedule can be up-dated as a consequence. We certainly think the

news will be welcomed by all Canadians, at least by those of them within range of television outlets.
Colour telecasts on an east-west basis can, in the opinion of hon. members of this party, make a great contribution to Canadian unity and will be particularly valuable in centennial year. Hopefully, the new medium will provide a great opportunity for Canadians from coast to coast to experience in living colour, as the phrase goes, the beauties of this land in all its provinces and all its various regions. In addition, the colour telecasting of many of the great centennial pageants and programs which are planned should serve to inspire all of us with the love for Canada which we all hold, but all too seldom express.
However, colour production is not the be all and the end all of television programming, and we would urge that the government proceed with all possible haste in extending television service to the north and to those other regions which are currently under-serviced. This, we believe, is a primary priority. As I say, while welcoming the announcement with respect to colour broadcasting we hope the government will proceed with all possible dispatch to cover those regions which desire to be included within the broadcasting net.

I had not intended earlier to speak on second reading of the income tax bill on the ground that most of what could be said had already been said during the budget debate. However, since that time the minister has introduced other legislation in this field which reveals rather clearly, in conjunction with the income tax bill, the economic philosophy of the minister and of the government. In the bank bill it became obvious that the minister's policy was to control inflationary pressures by a certain method. He had two courses open to him; one was that of a monetary course and the other was that of a fiscal course. He has chosen the monetary course.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I was interested to hear him tell us a few moments ago that the government had done everything in its power to control inflationary pressures. I presume he had reference to the pleas which the government made to subordinate governments and private industry to 23033-483
Income Tax Act
curtail expansion in their investment programs. I think this clearly underlines the fact that the choice of the monetary method of controlling inflationary pressures is not the most suitable means by which to achieve this end. I would suggest to the minister that had he been prepared to deal with this problem as a fiscal one, he might well be likely to achieve some success. It is pretty well recognized that the principal stimulus to economic expansion, and thereby to inflationary pressures in certain periods, lies not so much in the field of consumer spending power as it does in the level and direction of investment.
I should have liked to see the government tackle this problem, and the other problems in our society, in a fiscal manner. I suggest if the minister and the government are seriously concerned about the dangers of inflationary pressures, then there should have been a review of the level of the corporation profits tax, and a review of the present rather generous depreciation and depletion allowances in order that the drive toward growth and greater investment would have been to some extent curtailed.
After all, a classic method of preventing inflation getting out of hand is to impose taxes on the large corporations which, from their internally generated savings, are able to add to inflationary pressures by an expanded investment program. I would suggest at the same time that had this been done it would also have been advisable to have considered a revision of the personal income tax structure in the interests of equity in our society, and also I would suggest in the interests of some control of the inflationary pressures, because it is fairly well generally accepted now that additions to the purchasing power of certain economic groups, the lower economic groups in our society, do not necessarily lead to inflationary pressures.
Certainly there can be no argument about the necessity for a revision from the point of view of equity. We in this party have urged for a long time that the category of those who are exempt from personal income tax should be enlarged.
I want to make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that I am not advocating a revision of the income tax exemptions because I am well aware that if one merely moves up the limit of income tax exemptions, he profits those in the higher income brackets more than those in the lower income brackets. But I do suggest that means should be found whereby married couples, with an income of $3,000 and less, should be exempt from paying

personal income tax, and a single person with an income of $1,500 or less should be exempt from the payment of income tax.
There are a number of devices that can be used to achieve this without running into the difficulty of lifting the tax exemption levels for those in the higher income brackets. I had hoped the minister would have considered this before he brought in this income tax bill, particularly during the time which elapsed between the presentation of his budget and the presentation of this bill.
I want to underline again that if the minister is seriously concerned about inflationary pressures he will have to adopt some other measure than merely causing a rise in interest rates throughout the economy, because I would think it is a moot point as to whether this is really going to tackle the problem of inflationary pressure. It will have almost no effect on the investment programs of the large investing corporations of this country, and will likely add to the troubles of those whom he has not relieved in the lower income brackets.
So, Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that at some point the minister would have revealed that the government is, in the first place, really concerned with inflationary pressure, that it is also concerned with an equitable distribution of income in our society, and concerned with the problem of evening out some of the present injustices that are inflicted, not merely by the income tax structure but by the whole structure of our economy, injustices that the government could do something to alleviate.
I find the bill very unsatisfactory from that point of view but, as I say, I said most of this in the. budget debate. This bill, coming after the bank bill, reveals perfectly clearly that the government is concerned more with certain sections of the community than with others, that it hesitates-and the minister is hesitating now in this bill and in the bank bill-to impose any burden on those powerful interests in our society who hold in their control the power of inflicting inflation on the country, and economic injustice on a large group of our population. They are the power-fur members of our society, the more fortunate segments of the population, and it is very obvious that they are going to be protected by the government even at the expense of the ordinary citizen.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to speak at length at this stage because the items in the income tax bill

However, I wish to comment on the statement made by the previous speaker, who doubted whether an increase in the interest rates would contain inflation. I think it can be said that an increase in interest rates comes down to an increase in the cost of living. If an industry has to pay more for its borrowings it will pass the cost on, and the cost of living will suffer.
But I do not propose to get into a dissertation on taxing theory at this time. I know the minister has some amendments to offer once we get into committee, and I propose to make my further remarks at that stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the reason we have not brought forward legislation to implement all of the income tax resolutions is that the circumstances surrounding deferred profit sharing plans are very complex. I can assure the hon. member that the government adheres to the general principles laid down in the resolution. It may be we will find, after examining the great variety of circumstances which exist, that we will have to ask for an amendment to the resolution. I do not think that will be necessary; but we do want to be sure the legislation we bring forward does in fact deal fairly and equitably with the tremendous variety of plans which have been brought into existence in recent years.
Let me add this. At one stage we thought it might be sufficient to bring forward for consideration immediately only one clause of this bill, but then we felt it desirable to obtain as much certainty as possible in the tax legislation. We decided the alternative of bringing forward all these sections was the better move.
The principal change we felt had to be enacted immediately is that part dealing with withholding tax on the sale of securities of provinces and municipalities. In this regard there was some uncertainty in financial markets as to whether or not we were going to apply the withholding tax. The financial institutions outside this country were not as confident as we might be in this house that these resolutions would be accepted, and we felt it desirable to proceed at least with that part of the act.
It is our intention to proceed with the remainder of the resolutions when the house resumes in the fall, and I do not think the delay will be anything except useful to taxpayers in Canada.

May I just say a word on this point, really in reply to some comments made earlier by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. In fact, in the budget which I brought down some months ago and which is now being partially implemented by this bill, various fiscal measures were taken. The hon. member mentioned what he thought was the absence of fiscal measures. I am very glad to learn that the hon. member for Perth does recognize that some fairly stringent fiscal measures were included in that budget.
First of all, there was the restoration of the amount of the cuts that had been made in the previous year in income tax, because of the changed economic situation in the country. There was the application of the 5 per cent refundable tax on corporations. There was a reduction in capital cost allowance for undertakings which were proceeded with in the next 18 months. There was the progressive reduction in the sales tax. All of these were designed to exert pressure on the economy and to cope with the inflationary problem by fiscal measures.

There is also, and I have no hesitation in defending it, an appropriate monetary policy, just as there is in all parts of the world today. If my hon. friend looks at the United States, Germany, France or England, he will see this is a fact. The government of the United Kingdom, which is apparently of the same persuasion as that of my hon. friend, is employing the whole gamut of fiscal and monetary policy in order to restrain inflationary pressures. I think those inflationary pressures remain very strong. I believe we must employ all those measures we can reasonably employ without doing damage to the economy itself. Our purpose is not to stop anything, it is to contain our activity within our physical resources.

I am not going to ask the
minister to explain how the refundable portion of this tax is worked out because I believe it would take until tomorrow to do so. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we resume the debate on the amendment moved to clause 4 of Bill No. C-194, on the establishment of the National Arts Centre. The amendment proposes that, in the appointment of the board of trustees of this centre, due consideration be given the linguistic duality and cultural plurality of Canada.
In this type of debate, several points of view are expressed which reflect the particular experience and concern of the person voicing them. In each case, with the best intentions in the world, one speaks according to experience and personal interests; that is why no one person has any claim to absolute truth, just as no one errs completely. It therefore remains for each one of us to analyse the various points submitted and to adopt the attitude which seems most well-rounded, most realistic, most consistent with the concept or the ideal sought.
In the last few days, since the adjournment of this debate, I have had the opportunity and the time to analyse the opinions expressed to date, and if you will allow me, I should like to make known my personal views on the matter.
Let us say, first of all, that much more is involved here than a mere provision in a piece of legislation designed to set up a National Arts Centre. The very fact that this same discussion was held on second reading of Bill No. S-2 shows us in a dramatic manner that what is actually involved is the whole, essentially Canadian context of bilingualism, of national duality or co-existence, in short, of cultural policy, which our best Canadian
National Arts Centre
minds have been trying so hard to define for a century, but with new vigour and intensity, especially in the last ten years: an attempt at a definition which gave birth to the Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, which has led others to look forward to a constitutional conference, which has inspired the supporters of separatism, which has brought about the discovery of new stock phrases such as "associate states", "co-operative federalism", etc. Those are as many considerations which show a very keen awareness of this situation, of this experience Canada has gone through in the last century. It is essential that we should endeavour to define it, not so much to explain the last hundred years, but mainly to give direction to the next hundred years, because the peace, security and serenity of future generations depend to a great extent on the clarity of our definition.
In the present discussion on the amendment moved by the member for Levis (Mr. Guay), we have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and, among others, the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), the member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) and the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard). Previously, we heard the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) who, in his intervention of June 10 last supported the amendment when he said substantially that he understood the prime concern contained in this amendment, since that particular bill dealt with the National Arts Centre, an essentially cultural organization, where it was particularly advisable to emphasize the existence of French Canadians or, better still, the French fact in Canada.
It must be borne in mind that the minister said he would have preferred it if the amendment had not been moved. I entirely agree on this last point, but on the previous one I do not agree at all, because it shows a negative attitude which is harmful to the French Canadian fact, because it puts it in a defensive position from the start; it is forced to revert to a defence mechanism while the present generation, today's generation and the generation of tomorrow, whether French or English speaking, has a right to expect that we set the stage to promote its growth.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration put it quite well during the debate on the incorporation of the Ottawa Railway Terminal Company. It will be recalled that

July 13, 1966
National Arts Centre
there again, the discussion was on the advisability of ensuring French Canadian representation on the board of that company. I am quoting from page 2827 of Hansard, left-hand column:
The first thing that strikes me and to which I should like to draw the hon. members' attention is that whenever you insert in some legislation or constitution a clause such as this to protect a certain group, it is because you are assuming from the start that this group is incapable of looking after its own protection and of defending itself by other means. In other words, a form of discrimination is thus created to which I am completely opposed.
And later, he adds:
Otherwise it means, that to be represented in Canada as we should be, a provision will have to be included in every piece of legislation to ensure that such representation will be granted to us.
To complete this thinking, if I may be permitted, he should have added that, as far as existing legislation is concerned, past legislation, that is, where such representation is not provided for, there would no longer be any legal obligation, not even a moral obligation, since this apparently no longer is sufficient, to recognize the French fact in a practical manner. Is that not the true significance of the intervention of the Prime Minister when he asked the mover to withdraw his motion, and of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he asked the hon. member for Lapointe to give his assent to the withdrawal of the amendment?
May I be permitted to suggest, as an aside, Mr. Chairman, that if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration were officially to withdraw his support of the amendment to accept the suggestion of the right hon. Prime Minister, I feel that, in view of the judgement and the understanding he has shown several times in this field of national unity and of Canadian motivation, we would soon achieve the unanimous consent needed for the withdrawal of the subamendment and of the amendment now before us.
Generally speaking, I should like to note in passing that the wording of the present amendment is so vague and so watered down that it no longer means anything; the amendment recommends that "due account will be taken of the linguistic duality and the cultural plurality of Canada".
"Due account will be taken": This commits no one to anything and, for that reason alone, we should all agree to withdraw the amendment, since nothing can accrue therefrom, save confusion, misunderstanding and division. The Prime Minister first and then the Leader of the Opposition expressed their

concern that such a provision in a bill would divide our national groups, rather than contribute to the unity in equality which we are all seeking. I share that view and, in turn, I am asking the hon. members to give unanimous consent to the withdrawal of the amendment and subamendment.
In fact, in spite of the care taken by the writer of the amendment to hide under vague words the principle to be established, it is obvious, particularly in the light of the remarks made by the hon. members for Verdun, Lapointe, Sherbrooke and Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), that the purpose thereof is again to ensure by legislation that the French shall be represented on the board of directors of the National Arts Centre or any other government agency. Therefore, it is the whole question of the nation's bilingual character or, more precisely, the whole question of the French fact that comes up, and I think there is every advantage for us to consider this debate in this light, because we are putting a finger on and squarely tackling the problem which concerns all Canadians at this time.

In all honesty and objectivity I cannot see what this amendment, or any insistance on establishing a percentage of French speaking or bilingual representation on boards, can accomplish besides attempting to reduce this whole problem of national unity to a mathematical formula, which is no solution at all. Because it is restrictive and selective, it is essentially a negative approach.
I now speak as one who has spent more than half of his life as a member of the French speaking minority in Ontario, where I believe a more positive approach, through many years of sacrifice, effort and stubbornness as well as patience, perseverance and self-determination has resulted in the French speaking element penetrating more and more into every phase of economic, social, cultural and academic life, and in the English speaking element re-examining its whole conception of Canadianism and learning to seek out the differences in characteristics which explain our reactions and attitudes.
Mind you, I do not mean to suggest that life has always been a bed of roses, nor do I suggest that this battle has been won. We have had to scale some almost insurmountable difficulties, in education particularly, and circumstances still come up when strong stands have to be taken by an alert French speaking group, stands that can be and are debated at their full face value without
July 13, 1966

awakening all kinds of emotional stresses and strains. Personally, I have never felt that anyone was out to get me, so to speak, and I am sure that in those 25 odd years which I spent in Ontario never at any time did we, as a group or as individuals, take a step backward. French minorities outside of Quebec have been alert and alive, but throughout the tough moments of their experience they conscientiously exercised the same kind of patience which they expected of others, practised the same kind of understanding which they continually demanded of others, and requested the same kind of respect which they offered to others. The United States of America is a unilingual country-English,-despite the fact that there are there just as many groups and backgrounds or more than there are in Canada. That does not say that every Canadian must speak English or French. Nor does it mean that whenever there are two or three English speaking families living in a little village in Quebec where everybody else speaks French they must be given at state expense the opportunity of English schooling and so on; or that when a few French speaking families live in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, or Manitoba or Ontario where the surrounding language is English, these two or three French families should be given at state expense a French language school. It does mean, however, that every Canadian from coast to coast should respect the fact that Canada is bilingual; it does mean that wherever there is a substantial

Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I appeal to those who support this amendment and subamendment that the time has come in this country in which all of us have worked through our adult lives that the fact of Canada should be taken-not for granted-but should be taken as a fact which no longer needs defensiveness and which no longer needs negative provisions in legislation. One is usually content with a beautiful display of roses, sometimes forgetting that roses always hide thorns. When the rose withers and its petals fall, thorns alone remain and with the passing of time they grow sharp and stiff and prickly; it is precisely of those thorns I am wary.

Act would be constantly upheld. I am sure the Prime Minister will leave some day. Who will then replace him?
Confederation is barely 100 years old. When time came to unite Lower and Upper Canada, the problem at hand was that of joining a French people and an English people to form a Canadian people. When confederation was signed in 1867, time was taken to include section 133. I see, therefore that the fathers of confederation had the courage to write down on paper what they preached. They wrote it down, most fortunately, for were section 133 not in the constitution, decades ago the French fact would have been completely forgotten, and even as well perhaps the fact that the country had ever had two cultures.
A while ago some hon. members referred to the question of plurality of cultures. I do not quite understand. It seems that there are various interpretations or, at any rate, I give it another meaning. The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) talked about it on June 28. He said that one cannot have five,

six or seven cultures. One's culture is based on one's knowledge; the greater the knowledge, the greater the culture. It is a matter of degree. The man who has a thorough knowledge of English with all the advantages this entails-and heaven knows that there are many-has a certain degree of culture. Another man, similarly endowed and having besides a good knowledge of the French traditions, knows twice as much and his culture is wider. But it is not a matter of three, four or five cultures. It is a matter of knowledge, period. And the sum total of this knowledge makes a culture. In Canada, there is something we apparently always want to interpret; that is the state of mind that prevailed here today.

This is a state of mind that must be developed here-we are not necessarily of French origin, or of Anglo Saxon origin, but first and foremost Canadians. That is the main point.

Only, like many people in my province, I find that we have been waiting for a fair treatment for 99 years. But we are not getting it. And I do not need to go back 50 years, because a bill to incorporate the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company was brought before us. Some thought was given appointing English speaking persons to the Company, but no French speaking ones. That is not ancient history, it happened recently. Now, we have a right to say: Well, the same thing may happen again, and if we all agree on the reality of bilingualism and bicultural-ism, we want the existence of the two founding nations of the country to be recognized and that appropriate action be taken accordingly.
I pointed out the other day that I had conducted a survey in a number of departments and crown corporations and out of 1850 names or so that I noted, I found approximately 325, but I may have missed a few, which sounded French, and I am not

even sure that all those people are from Quebec. There again, the member for York South reaches a conclusion that I do not find logical. He does not seem to realize that if we are driven to ask such things, it is because we have 99 years of grievances behind us and that we really believe in confederation.
It is because, next year, we would like the contract between the two nations to be renewed for another century. Only, we realize that in the province of Quebec, our young people, our young businessmen, are dissatisfied. They are probably more realistic than we were. Being dissatisfied, they must assert loudly their feeling of not having been treated as they should have been. Because a few of them take extremist positions, we want to prevent a divorce from taking place in the years to come.
Mr. Chairman, some responsible people in my province worry about the manner in which confederation will be celebrated next year. They are worried for the very reason that in many areas young people are found to be dissatisfied with the treatment they get.
As I said earlier, even though it is obvious the result of the vote will probably go against us, just the same, even if the only result will have been to force some of our members to make a profession of faith, which was done with some eloquence, and sincerity, by the way, by most of them, I think, it will at least have served to promote the cause of goodwill and national unity. I want it to be known that it is in that spirit that we are dealing with this matter.
I realize it is an extremely dangerous subject, Mr. Chairman, and I am trying to contain myself, because it is so easy to become excited and get carried away over such matters, thereby complicating instead of straightening out the situation. But what I should like to emphasize, for the information of my English speaking friends, is that when we of Quebec raise this question, it should be understood that we are not separatists; we are Canadians who believe in confederation and think it will not last if Quebec is not treated as it should be.
Those who take this for racism should take it rather as an instinct of self-preservation, a warning to all Canadians of good will that it is time this conviction which everyone proclaims so eloquently found its expression in action if not in legislation.
I would not object, for example, to voting against the amendment if the government were to tell us: Well, here are the names

Therefore, let us have proof that this principle will be respected and we will yield. We will then realize that we Canadians can accept understanding and national unity.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not take up too much time but I have some remarks to make further to the speech we have heard from the hon. member for Ar-genteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Regimbal), from the hon. member for York-South (Mr. Lewis) and from the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) who has just spoken. I was particularly impressed by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Klein) of Montreal. He is of Jewish origin and he has clearly laid down here in the house, before all the members, the treatment the minorities, whether English or others, are getting in the province of Quebec.
Now, regarding the amendment on which we will be voting shortly, I see nothing discriminatory about it. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) is to amend Section 4 of the bill by inserting the following paragraph:
In the appointment of members and officers of the corporation, due account will be taken of the linguistic duality of Canada.
We have been hearing about duality and bilingualism etc. for 30, 40, 50 years. We have heard plenty of words but we have seen little action. When the hon. member for York-South said, a while ago, that French Canadians, as a majority or as an important group in any part of Canada-
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

-should be given the right to educate their own children in their own language and culture.

The member for York South is right on that score. But I would ask him a question. He is a member of a political party which has been in power close to 20 years in Saskatchewan and his present leader, who is here in Ottawa, was premier of Saskatchewan.
I have relatives in Saskatchewan, French Canadians like myself, who have never enjoyed the school freedom which we grant the Anglo-Saxons in our province of Quebec. And the member for Cartier was pointing it out a while ago. How is it that in 20, or 17 years of power, a government in such a province as

Saskatchewan, could not give to the French Canadian minority the same privileges which we give-mark this: "in accordance with the law"-to the minorities living in our province of Quebec? And these are not empty words; we act along these lines. This is the law in the province of Quebec but it is not the law in the province of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he is aware that in the province of Saskatchewan between 1944 and 1964 we more than trebled the number of schools in which French was taught, from something in the neighbourhood of 70 to over 210?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION
speechtext: Were those schools fully paid for by the government of Saskatchewan, without any increase in taxes? Did the French speaking people pay for public schools and then have to pay for their own schools?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION
speechtext: No, my hon. friend should know there are separate schools which are paid for by the ratepayers. The government supplies an equalization grant which applies equally, whether it is a French school or an English school. In some cases, the separate school is an English speaking school and the public school is a French school. In both cases this equalization grant applies.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION
speechtext: There are not too many of them. In my opinion there is quite a difference between the schools in Saskatchewan and the way the school question is treated in the province of Quebec. I have relatives in the southern part of Saskatchewan and they have to pay double taxation because they have to pay for public schools, and then they have to pay for separate schools.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION
speechtext: My friend is wrong about that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION

But the way our compatriots are treated in the province of Saskatchewan bears no resemblance to the way we treat minorities in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, in our province the rights of the minorities are guaranteed by law. Not by words only but by law.
We are now asking here in Ottawa to get as much. It is not so difficult if, in fact, there is no discrimination. When the hon. member for York South says that there is a cultural

plurality in Canada, we agree. Of course, if I went to live in China, I would have to comply with that country's customs, while keeping my French language if I could. The hon. member comes from another country; he arrived in Canada in 1921 or 1922 and followed the customs of Canada. But a fact remains; Canada is a bilingual country; he recognized it. Canada is a country made up of two great ethnic groups; the Anglo-Saxon and the French.
Therefore, if that fact is recognized in the legislation, it seems to me that no one should complain, no one should be shocked, because the cultural and bilingual duality in Canada is recognized in the legislation. That is why we will vote, we want to vote and we are asking all Canadians, whatever the ethnic group to which they may belong, to vote so that the cultural and bilingual duality can be recognized in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my explanation will be short because the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has already explained it very fully on second reading. Therefore I need say little by way of amplification at this stage.
The bill, as I heard the Minister of Transport, say, is to protect the symbols, copyright and trade mark position of Expo. Expo officials are now in the position of having to undertake the licensing of a great many products, and we want to ensure through this amendment to the statute that they are in a position to protect copyright and the like, and that fraudulent material is not circulated to the public and sold under the symbol or mark of Expo.
